modules.title: GEO foundations
modules.blurb: What the words mean, and which number answers which question.

qs.q: Your brand is named in an AI answer, but the answer links to a review site instead of to you. In the standard vocabulary, what did you get?
o: A mention, not a citation
A citation, not a mention
Both a mention and a citation
Neither
qs.why: A mention is your brand appearing in the answer text. A citation is the answer pointing at your domain as a source. They move independently, and the gap between them is one of the most useful things you can measure: being talked about without being linked means the engine learned about you somewhere else, and that somewhere else is where the work is.

qs.q: What does share of voice actually divide by?
o: All mentions across the brands being tracked
All AI answers generated that month
All answers where any brand is mentioned
Your mentions last period
qs.why: Share of voice is your mentions over mentions of the tracked set. That makes the denominator a choice, not a fact. Add a dominant competitor and your share falls without anything changing in the world. Always ask what a share-of-voice figure was computed over before you compare it to anything.

qs.q: Visibility says you appear in 60% of answers. Recommendation rate says 25%. What is the most defensible reading?
o: You are often present but rarely the one being advised
The two metrics contradict each other
Your visibility number is inflated
25% of users saw you
qs.why: Presence and endorsement are different events. Being listed among eight options is not the same as being the answer. A brand with high visibility and low recommendation has a positioning problem, not a coverage problem — and the fix is different for each.

qs.q: A page ranks #1 in Google for a query. The AI answer to the same question doesn't cite it. Most likely reason?
o: The engine retrieves and selects its own sources, often from different queries
Ranking data is not shared with AI engines
The page must be blocked in robots.txt
AI answers never cite top-ranked pages
qs.why: The engine rewrites your question into its own searches, then picks passages that answer the question it asked. Classic rank is one input among several, and often not the one that decided the citation. This is why GEO is not a rename of SEO: the retrieval step in between is new, and you can influence it.

qs.q: "Average position" in an AI answer refers to:
o: Where your brand ranks among the brands the answer names
Your Google rank averaged over the period
The position of your link in the sources list
How many words into the answer you appear
qs.why: It is ordinal placement within the answer — first named, third named, and so on. Order matters because readers stop early, and because engines tend to put the recommendation first and the alternatives after. A brand that moves from fifth to second has gained something real even if visibility did not move.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT something a GEO programme can directly measure?
o: How many people saw the answer
Whether you were mentioned
Which sources were cited
Where you ranked in the answer
qs.why: There is no impression count. Engines publish no reach data, so everything is measured on answers the tool generated itself, not on answers real users received. Any vendor number that looks like reach is an estimate built from other data — treat it as modelled, not observed.

modules.title: How answer engines work
modules.blurb: Retrieval, fan-out, and why the same question gives different answers.

qs.q: You ask the same question twice and get two different brand lists. The most likely cause is:
o: Sampling — the model draws from a distribution each time
The index changed between the two runs
One of the answers is a cached error
Your account was A/B tested
qs.why: Generation is probabilistic. Two runs of one question are two samples, not one measurement repeated. This is the single most important fact about measuring GEO: one run tells you almost nothing, and any metric built on a handful of runs is mostly noise.

qs.q: "Query fan-out" means:
o: The engine breaks your question into several searches of its own
The answer is shown across several surfaces
Your prompt is sent to several models
Citations spread across several domains
qs.why: Before answering, the engine rewrites the question into multiple search queries and retrieves against those. Those intermediate queries are the real battleground: you are not competing for the user's phrasing, you are competing for the engine's. Tools that surface fan-out queries show you what the engine actually searched.

qs.q: A model answers a question about your company with no web search at all. Where did that answer come from?
o: Parametric memory — what the model absorbed in training
A cached copy of your homepage that ships with the model
Its system prompt, which vendors fill with company facts
The previous user's session, carried over by the assistant
qs.why: Models carry knowledge in their weights from training. That knowledge is frozen at the training cutoff, cannot be edited by changing your website, and is often where stale or wrong brand facts live. Fixing it means getting corrected information into the sources the next generation trains on — slow work, and quite different from fixing a retrieval problem.

qs.q: An engine retrieves your page while answering but does not cite it. Did your page affect the answer?
o: Yes — retrieved content can shape the answer without being linked
No — only cited sources affect the answer
Only if the page was ranked first
Only if the user clicks through
qs.why: Retrieval and citation are separate events. Text that entered the context window can steer wording, framing and which brands get named, with no link shown. This is why tools that count only citations undercount your influence, and why the retrieved-but-not-cited set is worth looking at.

qs.q: Which is the strongest reason a brand fact can be wrong in an answer even after you fix your website?
o: The claim sits in training weights or in third-party sources the engine trusts
Search engines cache pages for 30 days
AI engines ignore sites under a traffic threshold
Structured data takes a quarter to propagate
qs.why: You control your own site; you do not control the model's memory or a review site's summary of you. Correcting the record usually means correcting the sources, not just the homepage — and then verifying over time that the answer actually moved.

qs.q: Two engines give very different pictures of your brand in the same week. The best first explanation is:
o: They retrieve from different indexes and refresh on different cycles
One of them is malfunctioning, so its numbers should be set aside
Your site blocks one of them, so it is answering from stale data
Their sentiment models score the same mentions in different ways
qs.why: Each engine has its own index, its own refresh cadence and its own retrieval behaviour. Divergence is the normal state, not an anomaly. Any single-number "AI visibility" score hides it, so always keep the per-engine breakdown next to the headline figure.

modules.title: Briefing your dev team
modules.blurb: You don't have to build any of this. You do have to know what to ask for, and whether the answer you get back is good enough.

qs.q: Your dev team tells you: “We've blocked the AI crawlers in robots.txt, so we're not being used for training.” What should you check before you relax?
o: Whether the agent that fetches pages for live answers is still allowed
Whether the file validates, since one syntax error voids every rule
Whether the training data already collected has been deleted
Whether the file was resubmitted so the engines re-read it quickly
qs.why:
Each AI company runs several agents doing different jobs. One trains the model. A different one fetches your page in the moment somebody asks a question — and that second one decides whether you appear in the answer at all. Blocking the training crawler does nothing to it.

This is the most expensive misunderstanding in the field. Teams opt out of training, believe they have opted out of AI, and never notice they are still being read. Others block the fetching agent by accident and quietly disappear from answers. Ask for the verdict agent by agent — never accept a single “AI bots: blocked” summary.

qs.q: Your product copy only appears after JavaScript runs. What do you ask your dev team for?
o: A screenshot of the page loaded with JavaScript switched off
More structured data, so engines can read the copy without rendering
A larger crawl budget, so fetchers wait for the scripts to finish
A resubmission of the page, so the index picks up the rendered copy
qs.why:
Many of the fetchers that assemble AI answers take the raw HTML and move on without running your JavaScript. If the content only exists after the page hydrates, it may not exist at all as far as the answer is concerned.

You do not need to know how they fix it. You need that one screenshot. It takes a developer about a minute, and the gap between what you see and what it shows is the entire business case for the work that follows.

qs.q: Your pages take about four seconds to respond. When does that actually cost you a place in an AI answer?
o: When the page has to be fetched live: not cached yet, or the user asked to check it now
Always: answer engines rank every source by load time, so slow pages drop down
Never: engines answer only from copies cached earlier, so speed cannot matter
Only when the slow page has no structured data the engine can fall back on
qs.why:
Most of the time an answer engine works from its own index or cache, built earlier and at its own pace, so a slow site is not simply left out.

Speed bites when the engine has to fetch the page live: a page it has not cached yet, a recent change it has no copy of, or a user who pastes your link or asks it to check now. Those fetches run against a short time limit, and a page that does not answer in time is left out of that one answer.

So a slow site is not invisible, but it loses exactly the moments when freshness matters: a launch, a price change, a correction.

qs.q: Your agency says “AI crawlers can access the site, we checked.” What is the right follow-up?
o: Which agents did you test, and what did each one get back?
When did you check, and will you check again after each release?
Can you send me the robots.txt file so I can review the rules?
Did you check from more than one country and network?
qs.why:
“We checked” almost always means one request from one tool. The artefact worth having is a list: every named agent, allowed or blocked, the rule that decided it, and the status code it received.

A single pass/fail verdict hides the precise failure that matters. This is the one place where a confident answer from a supplier is worth the least.

qs.q: What does adding schema.org markup actually buy you in an AI answer?
o: Facts stated plainly enough that nothing has to be inferred
A ranking boost over pages that say the same thing without markup
A citation whenever the engine uses a fact from the marked-up page
Priority crawling, so engines pick up your changes within hours
qs.why:
Markup says: this is an organisation, this is its name, this is the product, this is the price — in a form that needs no interpretation. It buys clarity.

It does not buy preference. Nobody has demonstrated that schema causes citation, so anyone selling it to you as a ranking lever is overclaiming. Knowing that is worth more than the markup is.

qs.q: A vendor tells you that publishing an llms.txt file will get you into AI answers. How should you treat that?
o: Publish it if it is cheap, but it is a proposal no engine has committed to
Treat it as required: engines now skip sites that don't publish one
Skip it: engines read robots.txt and nothing else, so it can't matter
Use it instead of robots.txt, which AI engines have stopped reading
qs.why:
It is a community convention, not a standard, and no major engine has promised to honour it. Publishing one is cheap and harmless and may pay off later.

The reason this question is here at all: knowing which parts of this field are settled and which are merely hopeful is most of what expertise means right now. Treat a convention as compliance and you will spend budget on the wrong thing while the checks that demonstrably matter go undone.

modules.title: When the buyer is an AI agent
modules.blurb: Agents that browse, compare and buy for someone — and what your site has to offer them.

qs.q: An audit says your pages score badly on “readability for agents”, and also that agents are being blocked at the door. Which do you fix first?
o: The block — nothing above it can even be measured
Readability, since it affects more pages
Both at once
Neither; wait for more data
qs.why:
These checks stack. If an AI agent cannot fetch the page, every score above that point describes a page nobody reached. A readability score for a URL that returns a block is noise presented as data.

The order is: can it be reached, can it be found, can it be read, can it be used, can it be bought from. Report the first level that fails and stop scoring above it.

qs.q: Your developer asks whether it is worth publishing the small discovery files that tell AI agents what your service is and how to talk to it. Honest answer?
o: Yes — they cost almost nothing and almost nobody has them
No — AI agents ignore them and reads the human pages anyway
Only if you run an online store; for anyone else they do nothing
Not until a standard is ratified, or the work will be thrown away
qs.why:
These are a few small files that let AI agents address your service directly instead of scraping a page built for human eyes. Today they influence very little traffic.

They are worth publishing because the cost is near zero, the option value is real, and so few sites have them that being early is genuinely cheap. Say “cheap insurance” rather than “urgent”, and save your urgency for the things that move answers this quarter.

qs.q: Your security team blocks every visitor that isn't a person browsing the site. What have they decided for the business, perhaps without knowing it?
o: That AI agents shopping for your customers can't buy from you
Nothing: AI agents are not customers and never place orders
That you rank higher, since AI engines reward sites that block them
That the site gets faster for customers, since agents no longer load it
qs.why:
More and more, the buyer is an AI agent acting for a person: comparing options, checking prices, placing the order. To your website, it doesn't look like a person browsing.

So a rule that lets only people through is also a decision to turn those buyers away, and it is usually made by people who were never told it was a commercial decision. When the buyer is an AI agent, your security policy is your sales policy.

Your job is not to overrule security. It is to make sure the trade-off is made on purpose, by people who can see both sides of it.

qs.q: An AI agent is shopping for a customer on your site. What most helps it get your prices and stock right?
o: An up-to-date product feed, like the one you send to Google Shopping
More product photos, so it can see exactly what each item looks like
Longer product descriptions that explain each item in more detail
Customer reviews on every page, so it can judge which item is best
qs.why:
Agents can read your product pages much as a person does. The trouble is that the price, stock and options on a page often depend on what gets clicked, where the visitor is, or what loads last, so an agent can come away with the wrong one.

A product feed states each item's price and availability plainly and stays current. Most stores already produce one for Google Shopping or the marketplaces, so offering it to agents as well is usually cheap.

It will not decide whether the agent can finish the purchase (checkout is a separate hurdle), but it decides whether the agent gets the basics right.

qs.q: A competitor publishes a commerce manifest for agents and you do not. What does that change today?
o: Little right now — but it is cheap insurance as agent buying grows
Nothing, now or later — agents will keep reading product pages
They start to outrank you in AI answers from the next refresh
Agents start quoting their prices when people ask about yours
qs.why:
Honest answer: agent-driven buying is early and the volume is small. The reason to do it is that the cost is near zero and the upside is real if it lands.

Overselling this is how GEO loses credibility with the people holding the budget. Being the person who says “small, cheap, not urgent” about the right things is what gets you believed about the urgent ones.

qs.q: A check shows AI agents are receiving your bot-protection challenge page instead of your content. Who do you need in the room?
o: Whoever owns the CDN or firewall — usually not your dev team
Your content team, since the agents are being served the wrong copy
Your SEO agency, since it already manages how crawlers see the site
Nobody yet: agents retry until they get past the challenge page
qs.why:
Whatever comes back is what gets read, so a challenge page can be ingested as your content. That is worse than a clean refusal, because everything still looks fine in your own analytics.

The reason this one is here: the fix almost never sits with the people who build the site. It sits with infrastructure or security. Working that out early saves weeks of asking the wrong team.

modules.title: Citations and sources
modules.blurb: Where answers get their material, and what your logs know that testing answers can't.

qs.q: Across most brands, the majority of sources behind AI answers are:
o: Third-party pages you do not control
Pages on your own domain, led by the homepage
Wikipedia and a handful of other reference sites
Social media posts from the last few weeks
qs.why: Answers lean heavily on review sites, forums, press and comparison pages. That reframes the job: a GEO programme that only edits the client's own site is working on a minority of the surface area. Earned presence on the domains that actually get cited is usually the larger lever.

qs.q: Server logs show heavy AI crawler traffic, but the brand is rarely cited. The most useful conclusion is:
o: Retrieval is working; selection is not — the problem is the content
The crawlers are failing to parse the pages they download
You should block them: they cost bandwidth and bring nothing back
Citations lag crawls by about 90 days, so wait for the next quarter
qs.why: You have separated two failure modes that look identical from the outside. Being fetched and not used means access is fine and the material is not winning — an argument, evidence or structure problem. Had the logs been empty, it would have been an access problem. Logs are the only way to tell these apart, which is why testing answers alone cannot diagnose GEO.

qs.q: A log line claims the user agent ChatGPT-User. How do you know it is genuine?
o: Check the client IP against the operator's published ranges
Trust the user-agent string; operators sign it so it can't be faked
Check that the request carries a referrer from chatgpt.com
Check that it obeys robots.txt, which only genuine agents do
qs.why: User-agent strings are free text and trivially forged — scrapers impersonate AI crawlers precisely because they get let through. Without IP verification against published ranges, your crawler analytics are inflated by an unknown amount and every conclusion drawn from them is soft.

qs.q: Your citation report shows reddit.com as a single source. What is it hiding?
o: Which subreddit and which thread actually carried the influence
Whether the Reddit links in the answer still resolve to live posts
Whether the answer spoke about you positively or negatively
How many people clicked through from the answer to Reddit
qs.why: Domain-level reporting collapses the thing you can act on. "Reddit cites you" is not actionable; "this subreddit, in these threads" is. The same applies to YouTube channels and to named authors on publications — resolution below the domain is where outreach actually starts.

qs.q: Which pattern most clearly signals an outreach opportunity rather than an on-site fix?
o: A domain cited often for your category that never mentions you
A slow page on your own site that answers a high-volume question
A product page with no meta description and no schema markup
A competitor's page that ranks above yours in classic search
qs.why: That is a source the engine already trusts for your topic, where you are absent. Getting represented there changes what the engine can say about you. The other three are your own housekeeping — worth doing, but they do not add new evidence about you to the world.

qs.q: Why is "cited without being mentioned" worth tracking?
o: Your page supplied the answer while a competitor got named
It means the citation was broken
It indicates duplicate content
It only affects image results
qs.why: You did the work and someone else collected the credit. Usually the page answers the question well but never states plainly who is answering it. The fix is cheap: make the brand attribution explicit in the passage that gets quoted, not only in the header and footer.

modules.title: Measurement rigour
modules.blurb: Telling a real change from noise — where most GEO reporting falls apart.

qs.q: A tool reports 30% visibility from 10 runs. Next week it reports 40%. What can you conclude?
o: Nothing yet: 10 runs is far too few to tell a real change from noise
A 33% relative improvement, which is worth reporting upward
That the work is paying off, since the gain is a full ten points
That the engine refreshed its index between the two measurements
qs.why:
Ten runs is far too little data. The same answers come out differently from one run to the next, so 3 out of 10 one week and 4 out of 10 the next can easily come from exactly the same situation. On 10 runs, a true 30% can show up as anything from about 10% to 60%.

Reporting that as an improvement is not a small error: it is the error that gets GEO programmes cancelled when the "gain" reverses the following week. A ten-point move starts to mean something only on many more runs, in the hundreds rather than the tens.

Ask every vendor how many runs a number is built on. If they can't tell you, don't report the number as a trend.

qs.q: Vendor A says you have 22% AI visibility and vendor B says 61%. The most likely explanation is:
o: Different questions, engines and definitions: the numbers aren't comparable
Vendor A tracks too few questions, so its figure is the unreliable one
Vendor B covers more engines, so its 61% is the more complete figure
Your site changed between the two runs, and both numbers caught it
qs.why: Each vendor asks its own questions against its own engine mix and defines the metric its own way — some divide by questions, some by answers, some normalise against a competitor median. Cross-vendor comparison of absolute scores is meaningless. Compare trend within one tool, and never put two vendors' headline numbers in the same chart.

qs.q: You sell mainly in Germany, but your AI visibility is measured with questions in English, asked from the US. What is the risk?
o: Buyers in Germany may get different brands than the ones you measure
None: engines give the same answer in every language and country
Only the wording changes, since engines translate the same answer
Only the prices change, which has no effect on which brands appear
qs.why:
Engines build answers from the sources they find, and those sources differ by language and country: local review sites, local press, local retailers. A brand that leads in English answers from the US can be missing from German answers, and the other way round.

Measure in the languages and places where your buyers actually ask. A number collected anywhere else describes someone else's market.

qs.q: You publish a new page on Wednesday. On Friday, your weekly AI visibility report shows a jump. What should you check before taking credit?
o: Whether the new page is actually cited in the answers behind the jump
Whether the jump is bigger than the one in last week's report
Whether the page was shared on social media after it went live
Whether the new page is longer than the pages it competes with
qs.why:
A jump in a report can come from anything: noise, a competitor's change, a shift in the engines. The direct link between your page and the jump is the page itself, showing up as a cited source in the answers that moved. If it isn't cited there, you can't claim the jump for it.

Check the timing as well: a weekly report is a snapshot from a fixed day, and if its data was collected before Wednesday, the new page cannot be in it at all.

qs.q: This quarter your visibility rose by 10 points, while your recommendation rate fell by 5. Which number tells you more about sales?
o: The recommendation rate: being advised beats being listed
Visibility, since more answers means more buyers see you
Neither: a rise and a fall of similar size cancel out
Visibility, since recommendation rates are too noisy to use
qs.why:
Visibility counts the answers you appear in, even as the eighth name in a list. Recommendation rate counts the answers where you are the one being advised. Buyers act on the advice, not on the list.

So visibility going up while recommendations go down usually means you are mentioned more often while competitors win the actual decision. That is a positioning problem, and a visibility number on its own would hide it. Report both, and lead with the one that tracks the decision.

qs.q: You have budget to make one part of your GEO reporting more trustworthy. Which buys the most?
o: More runs of the questions you already track
More questions tracked, across more topics
More engines covered in every report
A clearer dashboard for the leadership team
qs.why:
Answers vary from one run to the next, so a number built on a few runs is mostly noise. Running the questions you already track more times narrows that noise, and it is what makes a real change visible at all.

Adding questions or engines without it produces more numbers of the same low quality: a wider survey of noise. Measure a small set properly before you measure a large set badly.

qs.q: Your dashboard reports AI visibility to one decimal place, refreshed daily, built from five runs of each question. In measurement terms, that is:
o: Precisely wrong
Roughly right
Both precise and accurate
Neither precise nor accurate
qs.why:
Precision is how finely you report. Accuracy is whether you are anywhere near the truth. Five runs cannot support a decimal place, so the decimal is decoration — it makes a noisy number look authoritative, which is worse than looking noisy.

Roughly right beats precisely wrong. A wide range, honestly stated, leads to better decisions than a sharp number that is confidently off.

qs.q: Attribution asks which touch produced the sale. For AI answers, the question you can actually answer is:
o: Were we present at the points where the decision got made?
Which engine converted best?
What was the last click before the purchase?
Which question drove the revenue?
qs.why:
There is no click to attribute, no referrer to follow and no impression count. What you can establish is presence: were we named, were we cited, on the questions that matter, consistently, over time.

Contribution is provable where attribution is not. Anyone promising you attribution for AI answers is promising something the channel does not emit.

qs.q: Your tool tracks single, fixed questions. Real buyers ask one question, then narrow it down over several messages. What does the fixed question miss?
o: How the brands named change as the buyer narrows the request
Nothing: engines name the same brands however the chat unfolds
Only the wording, since engines ignore what was said earlier
Only the tone of the answers, which is not worth measuring
qs.why:
Most buying conversations don't stop at the first answer. People add what matters to them: a budget, a team size, a feature they can't do without. Each follow-up can change which brands get named, and the ones still standing at the end are the ones that get bought.

A single fixed question measures the opening answer only. A brand can look strong there and drop out by the third message, or the other way round. Ask whether your measurement follows the conversation or stops after the first reply.

qs.q: A vendor shows you AI visibility numbers. Which question tells you most about whether they match what your buyers actually see?
o: Do you collect answers from the engines' apps, or only from their APIs?
How many engines do you cover, and how often do you add new ones?
Can we export the raw numbers into our own dashboards each week?
How many competing brands and products can we track at once?
qs.why:
The app a buyer uses is more than the model. ChatGPT or Gemini wraps the model in its own instructions, decides when to search the web, may remember earlier chats, and can route the question to a different model version from the one a tool calls.

An API call usually starts from a bare model with whatever settings the vendor chose, so API-based numbers can differ from what buyers actually see. If the answer is "only the API", ask whether anyone checks the numbers against the real apps, and how far apart they are.

modules.title: The answer economy
modules.blurb: What changed in how people actually buy — and what the headline numbers are worth.

qs.q: Of every 1,000 Google searches in 2026, roughly how many end in a click to a website?
o: Fewer than 300
About 500
About 700
More than 900
qs.why:
Under 300, on SparkToro's analysis of Similarweb clickstream data across six countries, January to April 2026. The other 700-plus are research that never touches your analytics.

That one figure is the whole commercial argument for GEO. Most research now happens somewhere you cannot measure and cannot be clicked from, so a strategy built only around the click is optimising for the minority case.

qs.q: When an AI Overview appears, what happens to click-through on the #1 organic desktop result?
o: It falls by more than half, as many searchers stop at the Overview
It falls a little, by around one click in every twenty
It rises slightly, since the Overview links to the top result
It stays the same, since people still scroll past the Overview
qs.why:
Ahrefs measured a drop of about 58% across 300,000 keywords in December 2025, and roughly 74% of informational queries now end with no click at all.

Position one did not stop being valuable. It stopped being the same prize. If your reporting still treats rank one as the goal, you are tracking a position whose payout has quietly fallen.

qs.q: A survey of 1,076 B2B software buyers found 69% chose a different vendor than they had planned, because it appeared in a chatbot recommendation. The useful implication is:
o: Being in the answer can change the shortlist, not just confirm it
Chatbots are replacing sales teams
Buyers do not trust their own research
The survey is probably wrong
qs.why:
This is the line between GEO as a branding exercise and GEO as pipeline. The answer is not reflecting a decision already taken — it is changing it. One in three of those buyers bought from a vendor they had never heard of until the chatbot named it.

Which also reframes the job: if you are not in the answer, you are not in a shortlist that got assembled without you.

qs.q: That same research found review-site citations are buyers' top trust signal in an AI answer. It was published by G2, which sells review products. What do you do with the finding?
o: Take it seriously, and note who paid for it
Discard it — vendor research is worthless
Treat it as a neutral measurement
Use it only if a competitor publishes the same thing
qs.why:
Self-interest does not make research false. It makes it directional. G2 sells exactly what this finding recommends, so the honest reading is: real sample, plausible direction, interested author.

Read every number in this field that way, because nearly all of them come from someone with something to sell — this test included. Ask who ran it, what they sell, how big the sample was, and whether anyone without a stake found the same thing.

qs.q: A large share of visits that began in an AI assistant land in your analytics as:
o: Direct or unassigned traffic
A referral from the assistant's domain
Organic search
Social
qs.why:
Referrers are often stripped or missing, and people frequently retype or paste a link rather than clicking one. The visit lands in Direct. Assistants vary and this is slowly improving, but Direct stays a large and growing bucket.

So "we get no traffic from AI" is usually a statement about your measurement rather than about the world — and a rising unassigned line is one of the few early signals you have.

qs.q: Buyers increasingly ask the same question of ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude before deciding. What does that imply for your programme?
o: Consistency across engines matters, not just winning one
Track only the largest engine
Nothing — the answers are much the same anyway
Buyers pick one assistant and stay with it
qs.why:
Buyers treat agreement between assistants as a trust signal, and conflicting or incomplete answers as a reason to keep digging. A strong showing on one engine and absence on another does not average out — to a buyer it reads as doubt.

It is also why one blended "AI visibility score" makes a poor operating metric: it hides precisely the divergence your buyers are using to judge you.
